paragraphs.text: Split-hand/foot malformation (SHFM) is a limb malformation that affects the central rays of the hands and/or feet (Blattner et al., 2010). Gül and Oktenli (2002) described it as absence of the central digital rays, a deep median cleft, and syndactyly of the remaining digits, and noted that most familial cases are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. SHFM6 is a form of the malformation with autosomal recessive inheritance (Ugur and Tolun, 2008; Blattner et al., 2010).

paragraphs.text: Zlotogora and Nubani (1989) considered that a rare autosomal recessive form of SHFM might exist. As an alternative, they proposed a 2-locus model. In this model, the dominant mutation causing split hand/foot malformation is controlled by a gene at another locus, and a dominant mutation at the controlling locus leads to nonpenetrance of the split hand/foot mutation. Gül and Oktenli (2002) discussed both autosomal recessive inheritance and a 2-locus model for their inbred kindred.

paragraphs.text: Blattner et al. (2010) found a homozygous WNT10B mutation in a patient with sporadic SHFM. Nine heterozygous relatives had no sign of the malformation. The authors concluded that sporadic SHFM is not always a dominant trait. In recessive cases the recurrence risk is 25% for sibs and very low for offspring of patients, unless there is consanguinity. They recommended testing patients with sporadic SHFM for WNT10B mutations to determine the recurrence risk.

paragraphs.text: In a large consanguineous kindred with autosomal recessive SHFM, Ugur and Tolun (2008) used a candidate gene approach after homozygosity mapping. They found a homozygous missense mutation in the WNT10B gene (R332W). All affected members carried the mutation except one with an atypical, mild phenotype. paragraphs.text: In an Indian girl with SHFM, sparse hair, and interrupted eyebrows, Kantaputra et al. (2018) identified a homozygous 3-bp deletion in the WNT10B gene (c.695_697delACA). The deletion was predicted to remove asn232 in frame (Asn232del). Protein modeling suggested that losing this residue at a critical position would severely affect protein structure and function. The deletion was likely to shorten the protein's lifetime and prevent it from binding its receptors and other ligands.
